Pregnancy

Methergine and retained pregnancy tissue: what treatment can and cannot do

Updated: November 6, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Bleeding or pain after a birth, miscarriage or abortion can have several causes, including pregnancy tissue remaining in the uterus. Methergine is a name used for methylergonovine, a medicine that makes the uterus contract. Treating uterine bleeding is not the same as confirming that retained tissue has passed. The right care depends on the diagnosis, bleeding, infection risk and your circumstances: not simply on requesting an injection.

What retained pregnancy tissue means

Retained products of conception are placental or other pregnancy tissue left in the uterus after a pregnancy ends. This can follow birth, miscarriage or abortion, including after an earlier treatment. Retained placenta immediately after birth is a related but different clinical situation from tissue discovered days or weeks later; the same treatment rule does not automatically apply to both.

Possible symptoms include bleeding that persists, increases or returns, lower abdominal or pelvic pain and fever or unpleasant-smelling discharge. Some people have few symptoms. A blood clot, infection or normal changes after birth can resemble retained tissue. Neither the appearance of bleeding nor a medicine’s effect can establish the diagnosis at home.

When assessment must not wait

Get urgent maternity or gynaecology advice for persistent or increasing bleeding, fever, chills, worsening pain, foul-smelling discharge or feeling unwell after a pregnancy. Contact the treating team if symptoms do not improve as expected or you are unsure about the follow-up plan. If pregnancy might still be ongoing, report any vaginal bleeding promptly. Do not wait for a scheduled test or try another medicine to see whether symptoms settle.

Seek emergency help for severe or worsening abdominal or pelvic pain, or pain with movement or touch; pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion; heavy vaginal bleeding; or bleeding during a possible ongoing pregnancy with severe abdominal pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness. These are alternative warning patterns, not an all-required list. Do not drive yourself; ask someone to take you or call an ambulance.

How clinicians establish what is happening

Assessment starts with the pregnancy and treatment history, bleeding and other symptoms, pulse, blood pressure and examination as needed. Ultrasound, often a vaginal scan when appropriate and acceptable, may help identify tissue and its blood supply. Pregnancy tests or blood hCG measurements may be useful in context; a positive result alone does not prove retained tissue or mean that another uterotonic is needed.

If an intrauterine pregnancy was never confirmed, clinicians must consider a pregnancy of unknown location, including ectopic pregnancy. Other possibilities include blood clot, infection of the uterine lining, gestational trophoblastic disease or a vascular abnormality. Ultrasound appearances can overlap, particularly after birth. The team interprets the whole picture rather than using one scan measurement as a universal treatment threshold.

Waiting, medicines or a procedure

For a clinically stable person with confirmed retained tissue or an incomplete miscarriage, options can include planned observation, medication or a procedure to remove tissue. Bleeding, infection, pregnancy stage, scan findings, previous care and your preferences influence the choice. Waiting may take longer and may still end in another treatment; it needs a clear contact route and follow-up, not simply being left to manage symptoms alone.

Guidelines for early miscarriage distinguish incomplete miscarriage from a missed miscarriage: their medication plans are not interchangeable. Misoprostol is used in specified medical-management pathways, sometimes with mifepristone for particular diagnoses. Methylergonovine is a different medicine and is not an automatic substitute. Heavy bleeding, suspected infection or instability can require urgent hospital treatment, antibiotics and/or removal of tissue rather than another attempt at home.

What Methergine is

Methylergonovine is also called methylergometrine; brand names and available products vary by country. It is an ergot-derived uterotonic that increases the strength and sustained tone of uterine contractions. Tablets and injections exist, but strengths, formulations and authorized uses are product-specific. A generic photograph or a familiar brand name cannot identify the medicine you have.

US prescribing information describes use for uterine atony, bleeding and poor uterine contraction after delivery of the placenta. Patient information also describes control of uterine bleeding after an abortion. These indications do not establish that the drug reliably removes retained pregnancy tissue. Ask which diagnosed problem it is being used for, what benefit is expected and how success will be checked.

Why the context changes its role

A product label and a current clinical guideline answer different questions. WHO’s 2025 postpartum-haemorrhage guidance no longer recommends ergometrine/methylergometrine for routine prevention of postpartum haemorrhage. In treatment of established haemorrhage, selected second-line uterotonics may still be considered by the clinical team when first-line treatment is unavailable or ineffective, taking contraindications into account.

For a placenta still retained immediately after birth, WHO recommends a uterotonic only when postpartum haemorrhage is present and advises avoiding ergometrine because strong sustained contractions may delay placental expulsion. This is not permission to choose or combine drugs yourself. Methylergonovine is not a routine medicine to start labour, and an ongoing pregnancy is a contraindication in its US label; narrow supervised delivery situations described in labels must not be turned into home induction advice.

Supervision and checking the actual prescription

An injection requires a trained clinician, an appropriate setting and monitoring. US labeling warns against routine intravenous use because sudden severe hypertension and cerebrovascular events can occur; exceptional emergency use is a specialist decision. This article provides no injection technique, route choice or dose schedule. Never use someone else’s supply or repeat treatment because bleeding continues without contacting the team.

Before leaving care, check the exact generic name, formulation, reason for treatment, prescribed duration and whom to call about symptoms. If tablets are prescribed, follow that prescription and ask a pharmacist about a missed dose rather than doubling it. Tell the team if you are still pregnant or the pregnancy location or outcome has not been established.

Who needs particular caution or a different medicine

Hypertension, pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, ongoing pregnancy and a previous allergic reaction to the drug are important contraindications in relevant labeling. Tell the clinician about high blood pressure now or in the pregnancy, even if you feel well. Do not assume that a medicine used for someone else’s bleeding is appropriate for you.

Heart or blood-vessel disease, risk factors for coronary disease, sepsis and liver or kidney impairment also need assessment. The medicine can constrict blood vessels, and susceptibility to reduced blood flow matters. The team must weigh these risks against the reason for treatment and available alternatives; neither a low dose nor the absence of past symptoms guarantees safety.

Medicines and products to disclose

Give the clinician or pharmacist a complete list of prescribed medicines, non-prescription products and supplements. Some antibiotics, antifungals and HIV medicines that inhibit CYP3A4 can increase the risk of serious ergot-related effects. Other ergot medicines, vasoconstrictors and some blood-pressure or heart medicines can also matter. Grapefruit may be relevant to the product’s interaction advice.

Do not stop a needed antibiotic or chronic treatment yourself, or use this short list to declare a combination safe. Ask the pharmacist to check your actual products and recent doses. The safest response to a possible interaction is a treatment plan from the team, not spacing medicines arbitrarily or trying to counteract an adverse effect with another product.

Side effects and warning symptoms

Abdominal cramping, nausea or vomiting can occur, and raised blood pressure is a recognized adverse effect. Headache or symptoms after a dose should be reported promptly, particularly if severe or persistent. Not every symptom after treatment is a drug effect: bleeding, infection and pregnancy-related complications still need consideration.

Get emergency help for chest pain, serious breathing difficulty, a seizure, sudden weakness or trouble speaking, fainting or loss of consciousness. A severe headache that persists, new visual changes, a racing or irregular heartbeat, or painful, cold or numb limbs also needs immediate medical assessment; use emergency services if severe or accompanied by chest pain, breathlessness or faintness. Do not take another dose while seeking urgent advice about a suspected serious reaction. Bring the medicine packaging and do not drive yourself in an emergency.

A severe allergic reaction is an emergency

Stop the medicine and call emergency services for sudden swelling of the lips, mouth, tongue or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing; blue, grey or unusually pale colour; sudden marked confusion; sudden drowsiness or dizziness; or fainting or loss of consciousness. A rash need not be present, and the signs do not all have to occur together.

Use a prescribed adrenaline auto-injector according to its instructions and call an ambulance. Lie down; if still pregnant, lie on your left side. Do not stand or walk during a serious allergic reaction. Follow the emergency operator’s instructions, including if breathing makes position changes necessary, and do not drive yourself.

Breastfeeding needs an explicit plan

The US product label advises not breastfeeding during methylergonovine treatment and for at least 12 hours after the last dose, with milk expressed during that period discarded. Check the exact product and local specialist advice before feeding or changing a plan. If you need a temporary interruption, ask how to maintain milk production and provide appropriate feeds for your baby.

LactMed reports low milk levels in limited studies and explains that the US warning relates partly to unpublished infant reports after several days of treatment. Short early-postpartum exposure may be less concerning, but the evidence does not establish zero risk. Effects on milk production vary with the study and treatment pattern. Exposure does not mean that a baby is inevitably harmed: tell the team the dose times and feeds, and seek advice for infant symptoms or reduced supply.

Follow-up confirms recovery

Your team may arrange a review, a pregnancy test, repeat ultrasound or other tests depending on the diagnosis and treatment. Early-miscarriage guidance commonly uses a home pregnancy test around three weeks after specified management, with review for a positive result. A negative test does not rule out a problem when bleeding, pelvic pain or fever continues, and a three-week test date is never a reason to delay care for warning signs.

After birth or a procedure, follow the plan given for that setting rather than importing an early-miscarriage timetable. Removed tissue may be examined to help confirm the diagnosis or investigate other conditions. Less bleeding after a uterotonic can be encouraging, but it does not by itself show that the uterus is clear or that follow-up is unnecessary.

Future fertility and emotional recovery

Retained tissue and its treatment do not automatically mean infertility. Infection, ongoing bleeding and, in some circumstances, intrauterine adhesions after treatment can affect recovery; severe adhesions after an uncomplicated procedure are uncommon. Ask about the benefits and risks of the proposed approach and whether your history warrants a particular follow-up or procedure.

Recovery after birth or pregnancy loss is physical and emotional. Request an explanation of the findings, a written care plan, pain relief advice and support if you need it. If bleeding continues, periods do not return as expected, or you have concerns about another pregnancy, arrange a review. Needing further treatment is not evidence that you caused the problem.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Bring the pregnancy and treatment dates, scan or test results, bleeding and symptom history, and the exact medicine packaging to your appointment.

Ask what diagnosis is being treated, why the proposed option suits it, what follow-up confirms recovery and which blood-pressure, interaction or feeding precautions apply.

Write down the urgent contact route and act on warning symptoms immediately. Do not repeat injections, substitute miscarriage medicines or delay care while recording symptoms.

How BeMama can help

In BeMama you can record treatment dates, medicine names, bleeding changes, symptoms, feeding questions and follow-up appointments. This can help you prepare for a consultation. It cannot diagnose retained tissue, interpret a scan, choose or dose a uterotonic, confirm that tissue has passed or replace urgent assessment. Recording must never delay care.

When to seek help

Seek urgent maternity or gynaecology advice for persistent or increasing bleeding, fever, chills, worsening pain, foul discharge or feeling unwell. Emergency help is needed for heavy bleeding; severe/worsening or movement/touch-related abdominal or pelvic pain; pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion; or bleeding in a possible ongoing pregnancy with severe pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness. After medicine, chest pain, serious breathlessness, seizure, sudden weakness or speech difficulty, fainting or loss of consciousness are emergencies. Sudden lip/mouth/tongue/throat swelling, breathing or swallowing difficulty, blue/grey/unusually pale colour, sudden marked confusion, sudden drowsiness or dizziness also require emergency help. Follow a prescribed anaphylaxis plan, call an ambulance and do not stand or walk during a reaction; lie on your left side if still pregnant. Do not drive yourself in an emergency. These signs are alternatives, not all required together. Do not let symptom recording, a scheduled test or another dose delay assessment.

Evidence notes updated: November 6, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Retained tissue needs a diagnosis; symptoms, clots and ultrasound findings can overlap.
  • Methylergonovine controls selected uterine bleeding problems; it does not guarantee tissue clearance.
  • Observation, medicines and procedures are different options chosen for the actual condition.
  • Blood pressure, cardiovascular risks, interactions and breastfeeding can change the plan.
  • Follow-up matters even if bleeding improves, and emergency symptoms must not wait.

Frequently asked questions

Will a Methergine injection definitely expel retained tissue?

No. A uterine contraction or reduced bleeding does not confirm that all tissue has passed. The drug may be used for a specific bleeding problem, but retained tissue can require observation, a different medical pathway or a procedure, with follow-up to check recovery.

How do I know whether I have retained pregnancy tissue?

Persistent or increasing bleeding, pain, fever or foul discharge warrant assessment, but none proves the diagnosis alone. Clinicians use the history, examination and appropriate tests or ultrasound; clot, infection and other conditions can look similar. An ectopic pregnancy must be considered if an intrauterine pregnancy was never confirmed.

Is this the same as misoprostol or a labour-induction medicine?

No. Methylergonovine and misoprostol are different medicines with different uses and precautions. Early-miscarriage regimens depend on the diagnosis. Do not substitute, combine or use them to start labour yourself; ongoing pregnancy is a contraindication for methylergonovine in its US label.

Can I choose to wait instead of having treatment?

Sometimes planned observation is an option if you are clinically stable and the diagnosis is established. Your bleeding, infection risk, pregnancy context, preferences and ability to obtain follow-up matter. Heavy bleeding, instability or infection can make waiting unsafe; ask for a specific plan and emergency contact route.

What must I tell the team before taking it?

Tell them about hypertension or pre-eclampsia, any ongoing pregnancy, allergy, heart or vascular disease, liver or kidney problems, infection and every medicine or supplement you use. Have a pharmacist check interactions and confirm the exact product, purpose and prescription. Do not self-inject or double doses.

Can I breastfeed after treatment?

Ask for a plan for your exact product. The US label advises no breastfeeding during treatment or for at least 12 hours after the last dose, with milk expressed during that interval discarded. LactMed describes limited evidence and low measured milk levels, rather than inevitable infant harm or a zero-risk guarantee. Discuss feeds, expressing, supply and any infant symptoms with the team.

Does less bleeding mean I can cancel follow-up?

No. Less bleeding does not establish tissue clearance. Keep the planned review or tests, and contact the team for continuing bleeding, pain or fever even if a pregnancy test is negative. Do not wait for a three-week test or routine appointment when symptoms worsen.

Which symptoms need emergency help?

Heavy bleeding; severe or worsening abdominal/pelvic pain or pain with movement or touch; pelvic pain with faintness, dizziness, fainting or loss of consciousness, shoulder-tip pain, breathing difficulty or new confusion; or pregnancy bleeding with severe pain, shoulder pain, nausea, faintness, dizziness or loss of consciousness needs emergency assessment. So do serious allergic signs, chest pain, serious breathlessness, seizures or sudden neurological symptoms after medicine. These are alternatives, not an all-required list. Do not drive yourself; use another driver or an ambulance.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
